lead.t: Hepatorenal syndrome (HRS) is a functional, rapidly progressive renal failure that occurs in patients with advanced chronic liver disease (usually cirrhosis) or acute severe liver injury, in the absence of intrinsic kidney pathology.

b: Renal failure in severe liver disease WITHOUT intrinsic kidney disease - Excluded: concomitant liver + kidney damage, ATN secondary to circulatory collapse - Pathogenesis: vasoconstriction → decreased renal blood flow - Urine : hyperosmolar

qs.q: Which clinical feature is characteristic of Hepatorenal Syndrome (HRS) occurring in patients with cirrhosis?
o: Urine sodium less than 10 mmol/L
Marked intravascular volume depletion
Intrinsic structural renal disease on biopsy
Elevated urine sodium greater than 40 mmol/L
qs.e: Hepatorenal syndrome is characterized by a low urine sodium of less than 10 mmol/L, normal intravascular volume, and the absence of intrinsic renal disease. A high urine sodium would point toward acute tubular necrosis rather than HRS.

qs.q: What is recognized as the only definitive cure for Hepatorenal Syndrome (HRS)?
o: Serial large-volume therapeutic paracentesis
High-dose intravenous furosemide therapy
Transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt procedure
Definitive orthotopic liver transplantation
qs.e: Liver transplantation is noted as the only definitive cure for hepatorenal syndrome, although vasoactive agents and TIPS can be used as bridging or supportive measures. Diuretics are typically withdrawn.

qs.q: A patient with refractory ascites and portal hypertension develops renal impairment. Which specific laboratory finding characterizes Hepatorenal Syndrome?
o: Elevated intravascular volume status
Creatinine clearance above 80 ml/min
Presence of intrinsic renal disease
Urine sodium less than 10 mmol/L
qs.e: Hepatorenal syndrome is characterized by a urine sodium of less than 10 mmol/L along with normal intravascular volume and no intrinsic renal disease. An elevated creatinine clearance is incorrect since renal impairment features reduced clearance.

qs.q: Which finding is typically observed in the urine of a patient suffering from hepatorenal syndrome?
o: Alkaline with prominent glucosuria and high bilirubinuria
Hypoosmolar with massive proteinuria and high sodium levels
Isosthenuric with active hematuria and cellular casts present
Hyperosmolar and protein-negative with very low sodium
qs.e: Hepatorenal syndrome presents with functional renal failure where urine is characteristically hyperosmolar, protein-negative, and low in sodium due to intense renal vasoconstriction. Intrinsic kidney damage or acute tubular necrosis are excluded.

qs.q: A patient with advanced liver disease presents with oliguria, azotemia, and a low urine sodium level, consistent with hepatorenal syndrome. What is the underlying pathophysiological mechanism for the renal failure?
o: Direct bacterial invasion of the renal parenchyma
Obstructive uropathy secondary to retroperitoneal fibrosis
Primary glomerular deposition of circulating immune complexes
Marked peripheral vasodilatation leading to renal hypoperfusion
qs.e: Hepatorenal syndrome is driven by marked peripheral vasodilatation and effective hypovolemia, causing reflex renal vasoconstriction. It is a functional renal failure occurring in the presence of normal kidney structure.
